title: Angada in the court
hookLine: Rama's last offer of peace; the foot no one can lift
carry: dharma offers peace before the fight
last: THE NAME OF GOD CARRIES WHAT WOULD SINK.

cards: Two sides lining up for a fight: a group chat, a family feud, two countries at a border. Someone has to decide whether to talk first. The army has crossed the bridge.

They could attack at once. Instead, before the war starts, Rama sends one last messenger into Ravana's court with an offer: give Sita back, and there's no war. Not Hanuman, who already burned the place down.
Angada. Young. Vali's son, the prince whose father Rama killed.
And Angada walks alone into a golden hall full of demons, and faces the king with ten heads.

teach.b: Ravana knows Angada's father died by Rama's arrow, and tries to use it: why serve the man who killed your father? Join me. Angada doesn't take it.
He has chosen his side. The most well-known version of this scene comes from the Ramcharitmanas, the Hindi Ramayana of Tulsidas. Angada delivers Rama's offer, and the court mocks him.
So he plants one foot on the floor and says: if anyone here can move my foot, Rama will turn back. One by one, Ravana's great warriors grab his foot and heave. It doesn't move.
Not an inch. Finally Ravana himself gets up from his throne and bends to grab it. And Angada pulls his foot away and says, in effect: why hold my feet?
If you want to be saved, go and hold Rama's feet. Even now, the offer stands. In Valmiki's older telling the scene is different: the demons seize Angada, and he leaps up through the palace roof.
But both tellings agree on what matters.
Rama tried peace first. That's a real teaching of dharma.
Hindu teaching on kingship lists four ways to meet an enemy: sama, talking; dana, a gift; bheda, splitting their side; and danda, force. Force comes last.

Rama, God come down to set things right, still sends a messenger before he lifts his bow. Later on this path, Krishna will do the same, walking into a hostile court to ask for peace before a great war.
In Hindu teaching, a war for dharma starts only after the door to peace has been held open, and refused.

how: Angada's foot in Ravana's court is a favorite scene of the Ramlila plays of north India, often played for both drama and laughter, and it is recited from the Lanka Kand of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Both great epics send a peace mission before their war: Angada to Ravana, and later Krishna to the Kauravas.

o: dana: settling a conflict with a gift
danda: settling a conflict by force
sama: settling a conflict by talking first

games.q: the four ways to meet an enemy — tap the pairs.

s: Rama attacked Lanka the moment the bridge was done
first he sent Angada with an offer: give Sita back, and there's no war.
the planted foot comes from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas
it's the version many north Indians know from Ramlila. Valmiki tells the scene differently.
in dharma, force is the first tool a good king reaches for
danda, force, comes last, after talking, gifts and splitting the other side.

games.q: you're Rama. your army is across the bridge and ready, and Ravana is holding your wife. what do you do first?
o: attack at dawn while you still have surprise.
send a messenger with one last offer of peace.
wait for Ravana to march out to you.
games.why: he sends Angada: give Sita back and there's no war. only when the offer is mocked does the fighting begin.

practice: Think of a fight you're in, or about to be in: a sibling, a group chat, a coworker.

Before anything else is fired, find the one sentence you'd send as your Angada: an offer of peace, said plainly, with a way back for the other side. Say it out loud once, quietly. You don't have to send it yet.
Just know what it says, the way Rama did, before he ever lifted his bow.

wordCard.voice: Angada, Vali's son, who carried Rama's last offer of peace into Ravana's court, and planted a foot nobody could lift.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Angada, Vali's son. The word also means an armlet, a bracelet worn on the upper arm.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma offers peace before the fight. Even Ravana was told where to bow. That's fifty-nine.

sources.ref: Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand (Angada as envoy; the planted foot)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Angada as envoy, roughly sarga 41)
the four means (upaya) of dealing with an enemy: sama, dana, bheda, danda, in Hindu texts on kingship (e.g. Manusmriti 7; Arthashastra)
Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Krishna's peace mission to the Kaurava court)
